Sushma Soma on stage for ‘foreverest’ | Photo Credit: Ekansh Katiyar
In the early 20th Century, Mount Everest was still one of the last great conquests in the history of exploration. The Poles were conquered before the Great War but the first successful ascent of Everest was only in 1953 when colonialism, which spurred these adventures, was well on the wane. Since then, men and women, taking a page from Boys’ Own adventure books, have trekked their way to the top.
Over the years, the trickle of climbers has turned into a flood; recent photographs show long lines of summiteers like medieval knights besieging a fort. Many bring their own branding to the adventure — couple ascents, sibling climbers, even those with different abilities. “But Shri, my husband, climbed because he loved Nature,” says 39-year-old Carnatic singer Sushma Soma speaking in between rehearsals for foreverest , her multi-genre show, debuting in Delhi this Friday.
Sushma was born in Chennai and raised in Singapore and grew up walking the tightrope of living in a cosmopolitan city while staying in touch with her cultural roots. “I started music lessons at the age of four. I was surrounded by Carnatic music at home and loved it, but with a different diaspora and heritage around me, it felt irrelevant to my life at that point. I kept at it, though, going for classes every week under various gurus at the Singapore Indian Fine Arts Society. Then Carnatic singer Nithyasree Mahadevan came visiting with her mother, Lalitha Sivakumar. When she heard me sing, Lalitha mami said, ‘Why don’t you come to Chennai and learn from me?’ I had a six-month break between school and college so I landed in Chennai. It was for the first time that I met people who learnt Carnatic music as a passion.”
Sushma Soma has sung seven songs for the production | Photo Credit: Ekansh Katiyar
For a couple of years, Sushma traversed the bay shuttling between Singapore and Chennai while also graduating in Chartered Accountancy from Nanyang Business School and went to work for one of the big four accounting firms. She moved to India and met Shrinivas Sainis in 2013. They married the next year and moved back to Singapore. In 2017 she was introduced to her current mentor, violinist and Sangita Kalanidhi recipient, RK Shriramkumar. “The way he approached music made me realise that to live this way was a gift,” says Sushma, who was awarded Singapore’s Young Artist Award. She also began collaborating with siblings Mythili Prakash, a Bharatanatyam dancer, and Aditya Prakash, a Carnatic musician. By 2022, she had released HOME , an album that addressed climate change.
It was the following year, however, that was to test her mettle as a person and as a musician. Shrinivas was a data analyst, avid mountaineer and scuba diver. “In 2016, he went to the US to climb Mount Whitney, which kindled in him a love for alpine peaks. And one day he told me that he wanted to climb Everest. He trained everyday, and put his soul into it. Being surrounded by Nature was his switch.”
Sushma Soma on stage | Photo Credit: Crispian Chan and Wild Rice
In May 2023, Shrinivas summited Everest but never returned. Only his GoPro was found, the pictures in it a record of his time on the mountain. Sushma was in Singapore then and the grief of his passing and the lack of closure led to her losing her voice. “Our dog Latte passed away two weeks after Shri. People assured me that I should keep singing. That it would help me tide over the crisis. I swung between spirituality for the existential questions on life and science to find out why we grieve the way we do and what happens to our bodies. I found myself laughing even while grieving. I started writing a lot in Tamil and Singaporean screenwriter and lyricist Jaya Rathakrishnan, also a friend, said I should turn them into poems. Aditya stepped in asking if I wanted to set them into music and that’s how the EP ‘The Mountain Has the Last Say’ was released in 2024, exactly a year after Shri’s passing.”
Amanda Chong, another poet in Singapore, urged Sushma to perform it on stage live. “I mulled over it. I spoke to mountaineers on why they climb. I realised my pain was specific but it overlapped with others’ too. That was how foreverest was born.”
Sushma Soma flanked by Debbie Hannan and Aditya Prakash | Photo Credit: Crispian Chan and Wild Rice
The production that debuts at Oddbird Theatre, chosen for its intimate space, is by Sushma, co-written and directed by Debbie Hannan, with music direction and sound design by Aditya. The 90-minute production, developed in collaboration with Wild Rice, is in English and Tamil with no intermission, and brings together original music — Sushma sings nearly seven songs — theatre, storytelling, soundscapes and footage from Shrinivas’ final climb. “Aditya made me go back to discovering my violin and guitar, instruments I hadn’t touched in years. Through memories, unfinished conversations and encounters with Everest itself, I explore what it means to find my voice again while learning to live with loss. This production has come together because people have offered me their hearts and their stories in order to give mine a voice,” says Sushma, as she gets ready to introduce a brave man who strode along ridges and stepped into the brilliant light of the unknown.
foreverest is on November 27, 8pm at Oddbird Theatre, 9, Dhan Mill, 100 Feet Road, Chhatarpur Hills, New Delhi. For tickets, oddbirdtheatre.com
